NATO praised the joint Romanian-Italian response as proof of the alliance’s “24/7” readiness. by Kyiv Post | July 25, 2026, 1:00 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied This handout picture taken and released on May 29, 2026 by the Romanian Presidential Administration shows Romania’s President Nicușor Dan visiting an apartment block struck by a drone, wounding two people in Galati. (Photo by Handout / Romanian Presidential Administration / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip A Romanian F-16 fighter jet shot down a suspected Shahed-type drone that penetrated the country’s airspace on Friday, July 24 – the first time Romania has destroyed an intruding drone since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The drone was destroyed with an air-to-air missile at 11:02 a.m. over an unpopulated area near Padina in Romania’s Buzău County. No casualties or property damage were reported. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Romania’s Ministry of National Defense reported that radar systems first detected the aerial target at 9:39 a.m., approximately 20 kilometers east of Sulina on the Black Sea. It subsequently entered Romanian airspace and followed a trajectory through Sulina, Brăila and Fetești toward Buzău. Advertisement Two Italian Air Force Eurofighter Typhoons deployed at Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base under NATO’s Air Policing mission were scrambled at 9:48 a.m. Two Romanian F-16s from the 86th Air Base at Fetești followed at 10:56 a.m. Chief of Defence Gen. Gheorghiță Vlad later disclosed that the Italian aircraft had also fired at the drone but failed to destroy it. The Romanian F-16 subsequently engaged the target and brought it down near Padina. Fragments fell into a wheat field without causing casualties or damage. Romanian President Nicușor Dan noted that the area was uninhabited, allowing the pilot to fire without putting civilians at risk. NATO: Alliance ready to respond ‘24/7’ NATO’s Allied Air Command confirmed the joint Romanian-Italian operation following the airspace violation, highlighting the rapid involvement of aircraft from two allied air forces. “This multinational combined effort underlines how NATO is readyand able to react to any potential air threats, 24/7,” Allied Air Command stated, adding that the operation demonstrated the Alliance’s ability to safeguard NATO territory and protect its population. NATO noted that an investigation into the drone incident was underway and pointed to continuing efforts by Romania and other allies to strengthen ground-based defenses against unmanned aircraft. Advertisement The Italian Eurofighters involved in Friday’s operation are stationed in Romania as part of NATO Air Policing, while Romania maintains its own F-16s on alert – making the interception a combined allied response even though the final shot was fired by a Romanian aircraft. Suspected Shahed – origin still under investigation Romanian authorities initially stopped short of identifying the drone’s origin. Gen. Vlad told reporters that Romanian pilots visually assessed the aircraft as resembling a Shahed, the Iranian-designed family of attack drones extensively used by Russia against Ukraine. “Visually, the pilots reported the drone looked to be a Shahed type,” Vlad stated, while cautioning that it was too early to reach conclusions about its origin or purpose. An army source cited by Reuters similarly stressed that an investigation was underway to establish where the drone came from, while noting that Russia is the aggressor operating in the region. Romania has repeatedly reported Russian drones entering or approaching its territory during Moscow’s attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure along the Danube and Black Sea since the full-scale invasion began. Advertisement The July 24 incident also occurred amid intensified Russian attacks against Ukraine’s Odesa region. Vlad noted that strikes in the area have increased ahead of the harvest season, placing additional pressure on Black Sea energy and trade routes. Romania uses new authority to shoot down drones Friday’s interception follows years of debate in Romania over how its armed forces should respond when drones from Russia’s war against Ukraine cross NATO airspace. Romanian lawmakers approved legislation in February 2025 allowing the military to intercept and, when necessary, destroy drones that illegally enter national airspace based on the threat they pose to human life, property and national security. The legislation also provides a framework for allied forces stationed in Romania to participate under NATO and EU defense arrangements. The Friday shootdown is the first time Romania has destroyed such an intruding drone after dozens of previous airspace violations. The incident follows a more serious breach on May 29, when a Russian-made drone crashed into an apartment building in Galați near the Ukrainian border, injuring two people. Romanian F-16s were scrambled and authorized to engage drones during that incident, but the aircraft was not shot down because of the danger that an interception over a populated area could pose to civilians. Advertisement Friday presented a different scenario: the drone had reached an uninhabited area, the Romanian pilot had a safe opportunity to engage, and the F-16 destroyed the target while it was still airborne. For Romania – a NATO member sharing a roughly 650-kilometer border with Ukraine – the interception marks a significant shift from tracking repeated spillovers of Russia’s war to actively destroying an unauthorized aerial target inside its national airspace. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-bundeswehr.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IxbW Germany, like several European countries, has been rushing to expand military spending and to recruit new soldiers [FILE: July 20, 2026] Image: Mike Schmidt/photowerkstatt/picture alliance Advertisement Germany's Bundeswehr military employed roughly 186,700 soldiers as of July 31 this year, the Defense Ministry said on Monday . The increase is a relatively rare positive headline as Germany and its military try to ramp up recruitment, procurement and defense spending — to meet new NATO targets, appease the Donald Trump administration, and respond to perceived threats from Russia and beyond — encountering a string of setbacks and bottlenecks along the way . By the mid-2030s, Germany aims to recruit some 70,000 more full-time troops than it currently has on retainer, to reach a full-time force of around 260,000 plus around 200,000 reservists. Some, including Defense Minister Boris Pistorius , have voiced concerns that this might be difficult to achieve without reintroducing some form of military service . Defense Minister Boris Pistorius aims to set in motion an increase in troop strength in the region of one-third of the total German force over the coming decade Image: Uwe Koch/HMB Media/picture alliance What's the latest data on Bundeswehr troop numbers? The Defense Ministry said the total of around 186,700 put the military inside its recruitment target window for this year with months to spare It was aiming to reach between 186,000 and 190,000 personnel in 2026, and anticipates further increases this year It also said it was the highest total in 'around 13 years,' soon after the 2011 abolition of the country's former period of mandatory national service for many young men The total was an increase of roughly 3,700 troops, or around 2% of the total force, since the previous July Applications were also up 26% year-on-year, at 47,300 in total New hires from those applications rose 12%, to 15,400 Roughly 61,500 are career soldiers on permanent contracts The bulk of the full-time force, around 113,000 troops, are on long-term temporary contracts Short-term contract soldiers and volunteer forces' numbers also rose by about 6%, to around 12,100 in total Many members of the class of 2026 took their oaths on July 20 in a ceremony in Berlin, which is held on the anniversary of the failed 1944 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler, in a bid to remind new recruits of the German army's modern values Image: Mike Schmidt/photowerkstatt/picture alliance How are the new service surveys for young people faring? The Defense Ministry also published information on the new service availability questionnaires that are trying to boost recruitment among people of school-leaving age. A survey trying to gauge a person's availability, interest and suitability is sent to young men and women alike. Men are obliged to respond, women and people of other sexes or genders are not. At present, responding in no way commits you to any form of service, no matter how great an interest you express or aptitude you demonstrate. The figures do clearly point to the obligation to respond having a major impact on participation. New military service rules: Young Germans face tough choice To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Of around 194,000 men surveyed, 96% responded. But of 184,000 women and people of other genders questioned, only 4% voluntarily replied. The ministry said that if you excluded people who responded with a 0 when asked to rank their interest in joining the military from 0 to 10, then the average figure given was a 5. It said the questionnaires had led to 2,630 people coming in for assessments, and 865 people signing up for active service, starting either this year or in 2027. "This proportional increase in staff is an 'add-on' — that is, a supplement to the extensive recruitment efforts that have contributed to the very encouraging number of applications and hires mentioned above," the Defense Ministry wrote. Fewer than 1,000 of Germany's military personnel are currently on deployment, but all manner of tasks await closer to home — such as fighting and containing a major wildfire in the Hürtgenwald forest in western Germany late last week Image: Federico Gambarini/dpa/picture alliance Edited by: Rana Taha If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google , so you'll always see our verified news first. https://metro.co.uk/2026/08/09/two-europ.text: Two European airports are closing temporarily in 2028 (Picture: Getty Images) In 2024, Brussels South Charleroi Airport served more than 10 million passengers. But for much of 2028, no one will be passing through the terminals. That’s because it’ll be closing for almost three months – during the summer holidays, no less, between August 15 and October 31. The travel hub, which is the second largest airport in Belgium and serves both Brussels and nearby Charleroi, is getting a major runway upgrade. The 3,200-metre runway will be completely resurfaced, a move which is understood to come at a cost of €50 million (£42.8 million). Ryanair has a base at Charleroi, and it currently operates flights to the likes of Tirana, Vienna, Sarajevo, Sofia, Zagreb, Prague, and Barcelona. Wizz Air also flies from there, including to the likes of Skopje, Warsaw, Bucharest, Budapest, and Pristina, while Air Arabia and Air Corsica offer seasonal flights to Oujda, Ajaccio, Bastia, Calvi, and Figari. In 2024, the busiest route was to Bucharest in Romania, taken by 343,858 people, followed by Tirana, Bergamo, Budapest, and Manchester. Ryanair has a base at Charleroi Airport, as does Wizz (Picture: Getty Images/iStockphoto) However, there’s no direct flight through to London, which is served by Brussels Airport, operated by both Brussels Airlines and British Airways. According to reports in The Sun, all existing flights will need to be diverted, though there’s currently limited information on the interim plans. Trade unions are reportedly unhappy with the plans, as many are questioning whether the closure means all routes currently operating in and out of Charleroi will return afterwards. Other airports, like London Heathrow, operate a strict use-it-or-lose-it policy, which means airlines are required to maintain at least 80% of their take-off and landing slots if they want to keep them. This rule is in place for a number of reasons, mainly so the airport can minimise congestion. Airports are subjected to strict ‘use-it-or-lose-it’ regulations (Picture: Getty Images) The policy was waived during the pandemic, when countless airlines were unable to fulfil slots due to the lockdown and the resulting drop in demand. Since Charleroi Airport is also in the EU, it comes under the same use-it-or-lose-it regulation, which is European Commission policy. However, there are certain exceptions to the rule, which typically include when either a specific airport or an airspace is closed, rendering the possibility of fulfilling the 80% quota impossible. A spokesperson for Charleroi Airport told Metro: ‘A complete refurbishment of Charleroi Airport’s sole runway, together with other major infrastructure modernisation works, has been scheduled by SOWAER for the second half of 2028. ‘These investments are intended to ensure the airport’s long-term safety, operational performance and attractiveness. ‘To minimise the overall duration of the disruption, the various construction projects will be carried out simultaneously. This will require a temporary suspension of air traffic during the works. ‘We are currently working closely with all stakeholders to plan these projects, identify operational constraints and manage their impacts.’ Almería Airport serves the Andalusia region (Picture: Getty Images) Alongside Charleroi, Almería Airport in Spain will be closing its doors temporarily in 2028. For six days, all flights will be grounded to make way for a new and improved runway. At the moment, there are direct flights from London Southend Airport to Almería Airport through easyJet, which takes 2 hours and 45 minutes. There’s also a route from Gatwick, again through easyJet. The hub serves the Andalusia region, in the southeast of Spain, accommodating around 800,000 passengers per year. The area is a tourist hotspot, home to popular cities like Seville, Granada and Malaga. In 2023, approximately 2.65 million Brits visited, but despite this, Almería remains widely under-explored in comparison. Other European airport closures Charleroi isn’t the only airport closure that’s been announced this year. Last month, Coventry Airport in the West Midlands closed its doors. It was once a handy hub for travellers in the local area, with Wizz Air flying to various European destinations, including Poland and Italy, until 2008. Its runway was even graced by none other than Pope John Paul II back in 1982, who flew in via helicopter from Coventry. The runway will be getting a major revamp (Picture: Getty Images) But in recent years, things have been a little quieter, as the airport was only served by the Air Ambulance Service and private charter flights, which is what led it towards closure after 90 years of service. Meanwhile, for a period of time, Alderney Airport was the first – and only – airport in the Channel Islands. Built in 1935, the neighbouring islands were only connected by air when Jersey Airport opened in 1937 and Guernsey in 1939. Earlier this year, it was announced the airport would be closing to make way for a considerable revamp to the runway. At the moment, it measures 877 metres, and while the work will keep this length, it’ll widen it by five metres, from 18 to 23. The taxiway will be resurfaced, and the lighting systems updated so that planes will be able to fly in poor weather conditions without much disruption, as is currently often the case.
